questions.question: When scientists classify organisms, how do they assign them into groups?
options: By looking only at where they live geographically
By analyzing similarities and differences in their physical and biological features
By arranging them purely by how useful they are to humans
By grouping them only by their size and weight

questions.question: What is the correct order of classification groups from the largest, most inclusive group down to the most specific group?
options: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Genus, Species, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Genus, Family, Order, Species

questions.question: Compared to a smaller classification group like a genus, what is true about a larger group like a kingdom?
options: It contains fewer organisms which share more similarities.
It contains more organisms which share more similarities.
It contains fewer organisms which share fewer similarities.
It contains more organisms which share fewer similarities.

questions.question: What is the scientific definition of a species?
options: A group of organisms that look identical but cannot reproduce.
A group of individuals with similar features and genes that can breed to produce fertile offspring.
A collection of organisms that live in the same habitat and eat the exact same food.
A set of organisms that share the same lifespan and growth rate.

questions.question: In the binomial system of naming organisms, what do the two parts of the scientific name represent?
options: The kingdom and the phylum
The family and the order
The genus and the species
The class and the family

questions.question: Why do scientists sometimes examine organisms under a microscope to classify them?
options: Because some organisms can only be classified based on features at the microscopic, cellular level.
Because larger organisms cannot be classified using external features.
Because all organisms look identical from the outside.
Because cells always change their shape depending on the habitat.

questions.question: Which of the following features is correctly matched with the cell type where it is commonly found?
options: Animal cells - contain chloroplasts
Bacteria cells - lack a membrane-bound nucleus
Plant cells - lack a cell wall
Fungi cells - contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis

questions.question: How can cell features be used to distinguish a plant from a fungus?
options: Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose and contain chloroplasts, whereas fungi cells do not contain chloroplasts.
Plant cells lack a nucleus, while fungi cells have a prominent nucleus.
Fungi cells have chloroplasts for making food, while plant cells must absorb nutrients from the soil.
Plant cells are always prokaryotic, whereas fungi cells are always eukaryotic.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of using a classification key in biology?
options: To estimate the total population of an endangered species
To find out which taxonomic groups an unknown organism belongs to
To measure the rate of photosynthesis in different plants
To determine the evolutionary age of a fossil

questions.question: What does a classification key consist of to help identify organisms?
options: A list of Latin names arranged in alphabetical order
A series of questions about the characteristics and features of the organisms
A map showing the global distribution of different species
A diagram showing the internal organs of a dissected animal

questions.question: How does the classification system help scientists in their study of life on Earth?
options: It allows them to predict the weather patterns of different ecosystems.
It helps organise and make sense of the vast biodiversity of living things.
It prevents species from going extinct by changing their genes.
It provides a way to grow crops without using soil or water.

questions.question: When studying organisms in their natural habitat, what is a key practice for scientists?
options: Removing all organisms from the site to study them in a laboratory
Making, recording, and interpreting detailed observations of the organisms in the field
Changing the environment to see how organisms react to stress
Replacing native species with exotic ones to compare them

questions.question: If you are in the field and encounter an unfamiliar wildflower, what tool would be most helpful to identify and classify it?
options: A classification key
A measuring tape
A light intensity meter
A pH indicator solution

questions.question: When conducting fieldwork to observe living things, which safety and ethical practice is most important?
options: Collecting as many rare plants as possible to keep as souvenirs
Clearing away large areas of vegetation to make pathways
Working in a way that minimises harm to living organisms and disruption of ecosystems
Introducing new food sources to wild animals to attract them

questions.question: Why is a mule (the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse) not considered a distinct species?
options: Because it is much larger than both of its parents.
Because it cannot reproduce to make fertile offspring.
Because it does not share any genes with its parents.
Because it has a different diet from horses and donkeys.

questions.question: As you move down the classification hierarchy from Kingdom to Species, what happens to the organisms in each group?
options: There are fewer organisms, and they share more similarities in their features.
There are more organisms, and they share fewer similarities in their features.
The number of organisms stays the same, but they grow larger.
The organisms become completely unrelated to each other.
